info.description: An introduction to the tools of reasoning used in everyday life and in science. The overall aim of the course is to understand what makes good reasoning good, what makes bad reasoning bad, and how to do more of the former and less of the latter. Topics include: construction, analysis, and evaluation of arguments; logic and probability; updating beliefs and making decisions; designing experiments; interpreting statistics; identifying fallacies and biases. Open to all students.

ACADEMIC INTEGRITY: YOUR WORK, YOUR SUCCESS

At SFU, you are expected to act honestly and responsibly in all your academic work. Cheating, plagiarism, or any other form of academic dishonesty harms your own learning, undermines the efforts of your classmates who pursue their studies honestly, and goes against the core values of the university.

info.courseDetails:
What should you believe? What should you do? In this course, you will learn how to reason better—that is, how to make more thoughtful, informed, and fair-minded judgments about the world and your place in it. This course will not tell you what to think. It will not make you memorize lots of facts to parrot back on an exam. Instead, this course will help you develop general skills for deciding what to believe and what to do. You will learn how to construct and evaluate analytic arguments, avoid common errors in reasoning from data, and responsibly draw conclusions from limited information.

The course is divided into three main sections:
  1. Analytic Reasoning. This section will provide a guide to analytic argumentation, focusing on legal and philosophical arguments. Topics will include: issue-spotting in law and ethics, argument structure, arguments by analogy, and reductio arguments.
  2. Probabilistic Reasoning. This section will focus on drawing inferences from evidence and how to avoid common errors in interpreting statistical data. We will also look at the use and misuse of statistical data in the context of legal trials.
  3. Decision-theoretic Reasoning. This section will examine decision-making principles that often guide public policy, with a special focus on cost-benefit analysis and its limits. For example, how should we value human life (or extra years of life) when deciding how to allocate limited resources? We will explore certain paradoxes that arise in decision theory, including in the context of collective action.
